Title: Fine color guidance diffusion models application image compression extremely bitrates
Text:
Fine color guidance in diffusion models and its
application to image compression at extremely low
bitrates
Tom Bordin
INRIA
Rennes, France
Thomas Maugey
INRIA
Rennes France
Abstract—This study addresses the challenge of, without train-
ing or fine-tuning, controlling the global color aspect of images
generated with a diffusion model. We rewrite the guidance
equations to ensure that the outputs are closer to a known color
map, and this without hindering the quality of the generation.
Our method leads to new guidance equations. We show in
the color guidance context that, the scaling of the guidance
should not decrease but remains high throughout the diffusion
process. In a second contribution, our guidance is applied in a
compression framework, we combine both semantic and general
color information on the image to decode the images at low
cost. We show that our method is effective at improving fidelity
and realism of compressed images at extremely low bit rates,
when compared to other classical or more semantic oriented
approaches.
I. INTRODUCTION
Image generation has made significant progress, mainly due
to the emergence of diffusion models [1]. Those generative
methods rely heavily on computations and data in order to
produce the highest image quality. Therefore, when using
the most recent networks for other applications, it can be
interesting to avoid retraining or fine-tuning it but rather
adapt the models. The current popular and widely available
conditioning, done through text or image, is often not enough
for any applications that require finer control. Getting control
on the outputs without retraining thus becomes a challenge.
One of the difficulty of controlling image generation lies in
the fact that most recent models are trained to work in the
latent space of a fixed VAE, as proposed in [2], those models
are called Latent Diffusion Models(LDMs). By reducing the
dimension considered, the model can be shrunk, and the gen-
eration process can be sped up, but this comes at the expense
of interpretability and control. The solutions for controlling
outputs in pixel space are not always relevant for LDMs, while
unfortunately most current state-of-the-art models are trained
in this configuration.
In this paper, we focus on a specific type of control on
LDMs, we aim at generating an image that is coherent with a
given general color aspect which is given by a color map, we
illustrate the concept in Fig. 1, adding control to an already
semantic conditional generation. Control through color maps
Fig. 1: Two images generated with a Diffusion Model, con-
ditioned by the same semantics (rocky mountain and cloudy
sky). Contrary to the left image, the right image is obtained
by guiding the diffusion model towards a general color aspect
(top right).
can be a useful tool for image generation, especially in the
context of compression, where, a really coarse color map can
be used as a base to generate details. There already exist some
options available to control color for diffusion in the pixel
space, such as generating only the high frequencies using
a decomposition of the image proposed by the authors of
[3], or using a specific scheduler for the diffusion model [4].
However, to the best of our knowledge, a good control of
the color in LDM without training, has not been presented.
Some works propose training methods to add control to
diffusion models, by learning the directions in the latent space
associated with semantic meaning [5] or by adding a condition
as input [6]. However, we do not want to rely on training
or fine-tuning a new model on the specific task of color
map conditioning, as this would not take advantage of the
most recent models that could be trained in the future. We
want to focus on a training-free control that is adaptable to
any diffusion model, and in particular to LDMs. In SdEdit
[7], the authors propose a method that provides some control
over the color of the output using cartoon-like color maps,
but this control comes at the cost of a tradeoff between the
quality of the generation and the fidelity to the color condition.
arXiv:2404.06865v1  [cs.CV]  10 Apr 2024


Exploiting classifier guidance [8] which requires training, in
[9], the authors propose a universal guidance, with a training-
free method to control any diffusion models for any condition.
In the specific case of color guidance, we noticed that among
the existing methods, only a part of the information used for
control is preserved when guiding the generation.
We propose a new formulation of the guidance specific
to color map control. We rewrite the equations inspired by
universal-guidance [9], and show that, for color maps, con-
trary to the general case, the scaling of the guidance term
should not decrease during diffusion. We call our method fine
color guidance, we show that we make use of most of the
information provided by the color map, without affecting the
quality of the generated images.
Since the distortion perception tradeoff highlighted by
Blau.et al [10], and more particularly at extremely low bitrates
[11], compression has been taking a step back from the
MSE as a reconstruction criterion and focusing on semantic
descriptors [12], [13]. One way of depicting an image is
through a high-level color description, giving only a global
aspect of what it contains (e.g., a blue spot on the right, green
in the middle, blue on the top, etc.). Controlling the color
map in the generation of images becomes interesting in that
case. Inspired by the framework CoCliCo based on a CLIP
and color semantic proposed in [14], we propose to apply
our fine-color guidance to improve on image compression.
We compare the compression framework with another recent
generative approach [15] and a classical encoder VVC [16] by
targeting similar bitrates.
After a brief reminder of how diffusion models work, we
present the formulation of our problem in section II. We
then compare existing color control solutions in section III.
We present our proposed method for fine-guidance in section
IV and its application to image compression in an ultra-low
bit-rate framework in section V. Finally, in section VI, we
compare our fine color guidance with other existing methods
and their impact on compression.
II. CONTROLLING COLORS IN DIFFUSION MODELS
Our goal is to add control, without requiring training, to
any image diffusion model by using color information. Since
the latest models work in the latent space of a VAE, control
should also be available in these contexts. First, let us recall
how diffusion models work.
A. Diffusion models
Diffusion models stand as denoisers, starting from a random
gaussian noise, iteratively converging towards a clean signal.
With the popularity of diffusion models, the need for fast
generation and fast training has encouraged the emergence of
latent diffusion models [2], diffusing in the latent space of a
fixed VAE. In the following, to be more concise, we consider
that pixel space diffusion is a specific case of latent diffusion
where the VAE is the identity, see Fig. 2.

B. Formulation
Using an already trained and fixed diffusion model ϵθ, that
can generate images x0(ϵθ). We would like, through the use
of a color map c, to control the outputs of the model in order
such that the generated image has the global appearance of
the color map. We also would like that this control should not
come at the expense of the generative power of the model,
hindering the realism or quality of images. Control should
be achieved without retraining, keeping the parameters θ of
the model intact, but modifying the noise estimation, noted as
˜ϵθ(c) = ˜ϵθ(ϵθ, c) to relax the notations. The problem can then

III. EXISTING SOLUTIONS
Several solutions already address the problem previously
formulated, however, none of them satisfies all the conditions:
no-training, functioning for LDMs and minimizing the error.
We present the pros and cons of several methods in our context
and motivate the need for a specific method for color guidance,
especially in the case of latent diffusion models.

A. Conditional diffusion models
A conditional diffusion model follows the same principle
as a standard diffusion model, the main difference is that the
prediction of the noise is done over (zt, t, c). The condition, c
is then given as input of the diffusion model at each timestep,
with parameters θ trained to take c into account. Conditional
models are widely popular for text-to-image generation or
image-to-image generation application, however, to get a con-
ditional diffusion model, it requires either retraining a whole
network or fine-tuning an already trained one on the desired
condition. Which is something we would like to avoid in our
framework.
B. Enforcing colors in diffusion model
Given a diffusion model ϵθ, it is sometime possible to
enforce a condition on the output of the model, ensuring
that the output exactly follows our condition. For color map
conditioning, it is the case, but only when the diffusion process
is done in the pixel space, which means trained to directly
generate images from noise without the auto-encoder. Then,
for a given image z0, we can separate it as the sum of its
lower and higher frequencies uniquely z0 = l(z0)+h(z0) for
specified functions l, h, for instance, authors in [3] propose to
use a wavelet decomposition. It is then possible to enforce the
value of the low (or high frequencies) of the generated image
by replacing at each step the generated low frequencies by
our target c. With ˆz0(zt, t) the predicted z0 in (3), we edit
the value at each step, replacing it by:
ˆz0(zt, t, c) = c + h(ˆz0(zt, t))
(5)
At each step, the low frequencies of the sample are the one we
enforce, and only the higher frequencies are the one generated.
Enforced diffusion is illustrated in Fig. 3b, where vertical
movement in the arrow indicates the correction of the low
frequencies. This method is similar to the inpainting process
described in [18], where a mask is used to do the partitioning
of z0 rather than a DCT. This method can be used when the
constraint on c needs to be strong and when the diffusion
is done in the pixel space. This does not allow a trade-off
and to scale the proximity with the condition. Moreover, with
the popularity of diffusion models, the speed of their training
and sampling time has been a major concern and most of
the models are now processing in the latent space of VAE to
reduce the dimension, then, the same partitioning is no longer
available.
C. Initialized DM
Another method to control the generation of the diffusion
model is initialization. First introduced in [7], the diffusion
process can be initialized with information on the signal in-
stead of using a random noise. With this method, we influence
the diffusion process by giving partial information on the
signal we desire to get. In practice, it is done by starting the
generation at a later timestep 0 < τ < T with information on
the color degraded at the corresponding scaling of noise:

D. Guidance for diffusion model
Instead of initializing as in III-C, or replacing as in III-B,
authors in [8] propose to guide the diffusion at each iteration
towards an image that fits the color map condition. Moreover,
in [9] authors propose a method they call universal to guide
the output towards a condition without any training.
First introduced as classifier guidance, to condition on a set
of classes, guidance can be extended to any type of condition.
The only requirement is to be able to estimate the value of
∇zt log pt(c|zt), the gradient of the log likelihood of the
condition c given a noisy observation zt. While conditional
models (III-A) can learn to estimate this term separately
through classifier-free guidance [19], classifier guidance uses
a trained classifier to do so. A guided diffusion model process
is illustrated in Fig. 3d, the guidance correction is applied after
each timestep, iteratively getting closer to the condition.
The term for guidance comes from the parallel between the
diffusion model ϵθ with energy based models. Indeed, if fθ
is an energy based model trained to predict the log likelihood
log p(x), the corresponding training loss is formulated as:

V. APPLICATION TO COMPRESSION
The most recent diffusion models can now generate a high
variety of images with impressive quality [21]. When applied
to generative compression, they can either be used at high
bitrates to generate small details and avoid artifacts [22], and
at lower bitrates, they can be used as decoder using semantic
information for conditional generation [13], [23], [24]. Our
definition of color map IV-A, particularly aligns with image
compression purposes. Here, we propose to follow the pipeline
of CoCliCo [14] and we represent an image as a combination
of semantic and color information. However, to best harness
the information on the color that is given, we propose to rely
on our formulation of guidance to condition the generation.
A. Compression framework
The image is encoded into a vector pair σ = (σs, σc)
of semantic and color information, it is decoded using a
generative decoder conditioned on the semantic, and guided to
correspond to the color. The goal of the compression becomes
to generate images with high realism while preserving the
maximum semantic information contained in σ at a given,
extremely low, bitrate.
We call Φ the semantic projection of an image. The range
of the function Φ then defines a semantic space. We measure
the loss of semantic as a distance d in this semantic space.
Using this definition, noting E, D the encoder and decoder
xout = D(E(xin)), we can then formulate the problem of
image compression as:

where R is the function of the rate and Ψ measures the realism
of an image. Similarly to the CoCliCo [14] framework, we
want to minimize the loss of semantic while preserving high

function given by the diffusion model that can be influenced

B. Representation of the semantic
The image is encoded in two parts: the semantic σs and the
color σc. We already described the choice and motivation for
the color map, but we haven’t discussed the semantic yet. As
proposed in the CoCliCo framework [14], we choose to use
the foundation model CLIP [25] to encode the semantic of
an image. This choice is motivated firstly by the capacity of
abstraction of this model but also by its popularity. Indeed, as
CLIP is used to encode images and text in the same projection
space, this model has been an advantageous choice for text
representation in recent text-to-image models, which lead to a
large amount of available trained models.

VI. EVALUATION
We compare in this section several methods to control
colors, previously described. We show that our guidance can
be applied to pixel space diffusion, but more importantly, it
also performs well when applied to latent diffusion models,
outperforming current available methods on the latter. We then
apply our formulation of guidance in the context of compres-
sion in the CoCliCo scheme and show how it compares to
other extremely low-bitrates and semantic focused methods.
Fig. 6: Color guidance applied to pixel space diffusion models.
A. Performance of color control
1) Guidance in the pixel space: We showcase the guidance
for pixel space diffusion. We use an unconditional diffusion
model presented in [8] and pretrained for the generation
of 512 × 512 images. This model does not use semantic
information on the image and does not always produce realistic
images, but is sufficient to appreciate the impact of color
guidance. We show in Fig. 6 some images generated using
our guidance terms presented in equation (24) and universal
guidance (12). We can see that the generated images follow
the given color maps, with more accuracy than when using
universal guidance.
2) Guidance in the latent space: For latent diffusion guid-
ance, we use another model to compare the different methods
to control colors. The model we use is a LDM conditioned on
CLIP latent vectors as inputs for text-to-image synthesis. We
repurposed it for image-to-image synthesis using the CLIP
image encoder rather than the text encoder which refers to

We compare our fine color guidance with universal guidance

3) Discussion: Initializing the diffusion is a simple method
that does not require a computation of gradients, however,
this is a method that loses both in realism of generation
and fidelity to the color map because of the presence of a
tradeoff between both. Our formulation of guidance is similar
to the formulation of universal guidance, as both coincidentally
requires computing similar gradients. The main difference
between the two methods lies in the scaling of the loss. While
in universal, the importance of the guide decreases after each
step, we found that to optimally guide the scaling should not
decrease in √1 −αt but remain high instead because of the
ratio √αt/ ¯λt, the generated results confirm this observation.
B. Fine guidance for compression
We apply fine color guidance in the compression framework
previously described in Section V. The color map and the
CLIP latent are quantized to reach lower bitrate. The clip latent
is quantified using 1 bit per dimension, and the color maps’
palette are quantified over 5 bits per channel as in the CoCliCo
pipeline. We use the fine color guidance to preserve most of
the information that is sent inside the color map. We compare
our method to state-of-the-art compression methods, notably,
VVC. But we also compare with other generative approach
aiming at semantic compression rather than at the pixel-value
fidelity, such as Text+sketch [15]. We consider the generation
of images in patch of 512 × 512.
We evaluate our method on two configurations. One using
only a 16 × 16 color map resolution, targeting a bitrate
similar to the lowest VVC quantization parameter. And an-
other one, keeping more information on the colors, using a

The realism of generated images can also be appreciated

resolution of the color maps is an interesting parameter to
vary. We present in the table the rate per image rather than a
bit per pixel, to be independent of the diffusion model output
capacity since our description of an image does not depend

The MSE is here used as a metric of color fidelity and not
as an objective to optimize at all cost. The goal of guidance is

VII. CONCLUSION
We proposed a method for color guidance in diffusion
models, more specifically, for latent diffusion models that
does not require any training. This method outperforms other
training-free methods and can be applied to any latent or
pixel space diffusion model. We can then advantageously use
it on the latest diffusions models to control the output. We
showcased the use of our method in a context of compression
at extremely low bitrates, showing that a low resolution color
map can be a good descriptor to add to the semantic. We
show, in the context of the CoCliCo coding pipeline, that the
information given by the color map is better preserved using
fine color guidance, avoiding the waste of bitrate.

Abstract: This study addresses the challenge of, without train- ing or fine-tuning, controlling the global color aspect of images generated with a diffusion model. We rewrite the guidance equations to ensure that the outputs are closer to a known color map, and this without hindering the quality of the generation. Our method leads to new guidance equations. We show in the color guidance context that, the scaling of the guidance should not decrease but remains high throughout the diffusion process. In a second contribution, our guidance is applied in a compression framework, we combine both semantic and general color information on the image to decode the images at low cost. We show that our method is effective at improving fidelity and realism of compressed images at extremely low bit rates, when compared to other classical or more semantic oriented approaches.
